title: CDNs: answering from a city near the user
dek: How a content delivery network keeps copies close to your users, what decides whether it can answer, and why a live cricket match is possible at all.

items: A CDN is a network of caches in many cities. Users are sent to the nearest one, and it answers from its copy when it has one.
The number that matters is the hit ratio: the share of requests answered at the edge. At 99%, only 1 request in 100 reaches your servers.
Cache-Control headers and the cache key decide what is stored and for how long. Get them wrong and you either miss all the time or show stale or private data.
Live video works on a CDN because every viewer asks for the same few-second chunk, so one fetch serves lakhs of people.
Your origin still has to survive the misses: after a purge, at the start of a live event, and for everything that cannot be cached.

body.cap: Pune's edge already has the restaurant photo and answers in about 10 ms. Delhi's edge does not, so the request goes through the origin shield to Zotato's origin, once, and both keep a copy. When Chennai's edge misses a moment later, the shield answers and the origin is not asked again.

body.x: Zotato's servers sit in one region, say Mumbai. A photo of a biryani is about 200 KB, and the home screen shows forty of them. Sending all of that from Mumbai to every phone in the country is slow for users far away and expensive for Zotato.

A CDN (Cloudflare, Akamai, Amazon CloudFront, Fastly, Google Cloud CDN) runs servers in hundreds of cities. DNS or anycast routing sends each user to a nearby one, the edge. The edge keeps copies of what users ask for. If it has the file, it answers straight away. If not, it fetches the file from your servers (the origin) once and keeps it for the next person.

That gives you three things: pages load faster because the data travels a short way, your servers and bandwidth bill shrink because most requests never reach them, and sudden crowds land on the CDN's capacity instead of yours.

A kirana shop in every lane. Most of what people need is already on its shelf, so they walk two minutes instead of going to the wholesale market. Only when the shop runs out does the owner fetch more from the warehouse, and then the whole lane is covered again.
What to put on a CDN

body.name: Static files
body.what: JavaScript, CSS, fonts, images and app downloads: the same bytes for everyone.
body.use: Everything a page loads that does not change per user. Cache for a long time.
body.avoid: Files you update in place under the same name; users keep the old copy until it expires.
body.ex: Restaurant photos and the web app's `app.3f9c2a.js`. The hash in the name changes with every build, so the file can be cached for a year and a new build simply uses a new name.
body.like: Packaged biscuits: same packet for everyone, fine on the shelf for months.
more: Send `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable` for versioned files. The HTML that refers to them gets a short max-age, so a new build shows up within a minute.
Images are usually the biggest share of bytes. Many CDNs can also resize and convert them (WebP, AVIF) at the edge, so a phone gets a small file and a laptop a sharp one.

body.name: Video
body.what: Video is cut into small chunks (2 to 6 seconds each, HLS or DASH) plus a playlist that lists them. Players fetch chunk after chunk.
body.use: Video on demand and live streams. The CDN is not optional here: no origin could send the bytes.
body.avoid: Treating the playlist like a chunk. During a live stream the playlist changes every few seconds, so it needs a very short TTL.
body.ex: Zotato's recipe videos are video on demand: each chunk is fetched once per edge and served for weeks.
body.like: A newspaper: printed once, the same copy goes to every house in the lane.
more: Live streams are where a CDN looks like magic. In the IND vs PAK challenge, 3.5 crore viewers each ask for a 4-second chunk every 4 seconds: 87.5 lakh requests a second. They all want the same chunk at the same moment, so each edge fetches it once and answers everyone nearby.

Every new chunk still misses once per edge (or once per shield). That is why the origin of a live stream sees a burst every few seconds, and why it must be sized for the miss traffic at the busiest moment, not for the average.

body.name: API responses
body.what: Responses that are the same for many users and can be a little old, such as a restaurant's public menu.
body.use: Read-heavy public data: menus, catalogue pages, a list of cities served. Short TTLs (seconds to minutes).
body.avoid: Anything that depends on who is asking: carts, orders, addresses, prices with a personal discount.
body.ex: `GET /restaurants/r_42/menu` is the same for everyone in the area, so it can be cached for 60 seconds. `GET /orders/123` must never be.
body.like: The price list painted on the shop wall, not the bill for your basket.
more: Mark personal responses `Cache-Control: private` or `no-store`. Caching one user's response and serving it to another is one of the worst incidents a site can have, and it happens when a header is missing.

This site's own API sends `public, max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=600` for its articles: a copy can be up to a minute old, and for ten more minutes an old copy is served while a fresh one is fetched in the background.

body.x: Hits, misses and how long a copy lives

body.cap: One menu at one edge. The first request misses and fetches the menu. For an hour (`max-age=3600`) every request is a hit. At 8:00 the copy is old, so one request checks with the origin, which answers `304 Not Modified`, and the copy is fresh again. At 8:20 the restaurant changes its menu and Zotato purges it, so the next request fetches the new one.

items: Your origin decides, with headers. `max-age` is how long any cache may keep a response; `s-maxage` applies only to shared caches such as the CDN; `no-store` means never keep it; `private` means only the user's own browser may.
When a copy expires, the edge does not always download it again. It asks "has this changed?" with the `ETag` it has. If not, the origin answers `304` with no body, which is cheap.
`stale-while-revalidate` lets the edge keep serving the old copy for a while as it fetches a new one, so no user waits for the origin.

The cache key is what makes two requests "the same": usually the host and path, plus any query parameters or headers you choose. Add too much (a tracking parameter, every cookie) and nothing ever hits. Add too little and users get each other's variants.
To change something before it expires, either purge it (seconds to minutes, depending on the CDN) or, better, give the new version a new name.

body.x: Hit ratio is what makes the maths work. At 87.5 lakh requests a second and a 99% hit ratio, 87,500 requests a second reach the origin. At 95% it is 4.4 lakh, five times more servers. Each extra point of hit ratio saves real money.

body.label: Origin shield, request collapsing and the thundering herd

body.x: With hundreds of edges, a new file can miss at every one of them at once, and each miss is a request to your origin. An origin shield is one extra cache tier, in one region, between the edges and your servers. Edges ask the shield; only the shield asks the origin. Hundreds of misses become one.

Request collapsing (also called coalescing) handles the same problem inside one cache: when a thousand requests for the same missing chunk arrive in the same second, the cache sends one request to the origin and makes the other 999 wait for that answer.

The dangerous moments are when the cache is empty: a full purge, a new release that renames every file, a cache node restarting, or the first ball of a match. Avoid purging everything at once, warm the cache before a known event, and size the origin for the burst that follows.

items: Money: you pay per GB delivered and per request. For video and images the transfer is the big number. It is still far cheaper than sending the same bytes from your own servers.
Stale content: a copy lives until it expires or is purged. Decide per type how old is acceptable, and use versioned names where it is not.
Leaks: a missing `private` header can cache one user's page and show it to others. Review the headers of every endpoint the CDN can see.
Harder debugging: a response may come from the browser, the edge, the shield or the origin. Response headers such as `Age` and the CDN's cache-status header tell you which.
The origin is still there: it must handle the misses, the burst after a purge and everything uncacheable, such as placing an order.
HTTPS ends at the edge, close to the user, which makes the first connection faster.
The CDN's size absorbs most denial-of-service floods before they reach you, and a web application firewall at the edge can block common attacks.
Signed URLs or signed cookies let only paying users fetch a video, without the origin checking every chunk.
Lock the origin so it accepts traffic only from the CDN. Otherwise attackers skip the CDN and hit your servers directly.
Put a CDN in front as soon as the design serves images, video or other files to many users. Say what it caches and for how long.
Do the hit-ratio maths out loud: total requests × miss ratio = what your origin must handle.
Keep personal and write traffic off the cache; mention `private` and `no-store`.
For live video, explain chunks and why everyone asking for the same chunk makes it cacheable, then size the origin for the misses at the peak.
Mention invalidation: versioned file names for assets, short TTLs or purges for data.

body.x: 3.5 crore people watch India play Pakistan live. Put a CDN in front of the video servers and size them for the misses, so nobody buffers in the last over.
